title: Name it to tame it
hookLine: putting feelings into words calmed the brain's alarm response in a study by Lieberman and colleagues

lines: AN ANGRY FACE IN A SCANNER.
PICK THE WORD, OR MATCH THE FACE.
cards: Lying in a brain scanner, a volunteer sees a photograph of a face twisted with anger. Underneath it, two words: angry, and scared. The job is to pick the word that fits.
Another time, the same kind of face appears, but the job is to match it to another face, no words involved. It sounds like a trivial difference.
But the researchers, led by the psychologist Matthew Lieberman, were watching a small part of the brain that reacts to threat, and it behaved differently depending on whether a word was involved.

teach.b: When people put a word to the emotion in the face, activity in the amygdala, a region involved in the brain's alarm response, was lower than when they matched faces without words.
At the same time, a region toward the front of the brain, linked to putting things into words and to regulating responses, was more active. The researchers called this affect labeling.
Their reading: naming a feeling seems to take a little heat out of it. Now the catch. This was about other people's faces in a lab, not a real argument at home.
Later studies of labeling one's own feelings have had interesting but more varied results.

teach.h: A LAB FINDING, AND A QUIET ONE.
teach.b: And the effect is quiet; naming doesn't make the feeling vanish.
The psychiatrist Dan Siegel helped popularize a short way of saying it, name it to tame it, especially when teaching parents to help children with big feelings. And an older voice.

The philosopher Baruch Spinoza, writing in Latin in his Ethics, where his word for emotion was affectus, argued that an emotion which is a passion stops being a passion once we form a clear and distinct idea of it.
He meant something richer than a label: a real understanding of what the feeling is and where it comes from. But he and the scanner point in a similar direction.
A feeling with no name tends to run the show; a feeling clearly seen loosens its grip a little. Some teachers add a twist: reach for a precise name. Not upset, but disappointed.

how: Therapists, teachers and parents use affect labeling, often called name it to tame it, to help people and children put words to strong feelings; some meditators add a quiet mental label to what they notice.

games.q: what does “name it to tame it” mean?
o: giving a feeling an exact word, which can calm it a bit
talking yourself out of a feeling with logic
pushing a feeling away until it fades on its own

games.q: inside name it to tame it: tap the pairs.
p: putting a word to a feeling

s: in the study, naming the emotion went with lower amygdala activity
picking a word for the face quieted the alarm region compared with matching faces.
naming a feeling makes it disappear
the effect is quiet: it takes a little heat out, it doesn't erase the feeling.
the study had people label their own arguments at home
they labeled emotional faces in photographs, in a scanner.

games.q: you're in the scanner, looking at an angry face. which task goes with a quieter alarm response?
o: matching it to another angry face.
picking the word angry from two choices.
staring at it with no task at all.
games.why: choosing a word for the emotion went with lower amygdala activity than matching faces. the researchers called it affect labeling.

practice: Check the inside, heartbeat, breath, stomach, shoulders, then ask quietly what is here right now, and find one feeling.
Give it the most exact word you can, looking underneath fine or stressed for something like restless, tender, hurried or relieved, and say it silently once.
Notice whether anything shifts, even slightly; if nothing does, that's fine, and rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Name it to tame it. Putting a feeling into a precise word, which in one lab study went along with a calmer alarm response in the brain. Today's word.

orig.note: Spinoza's Latin word in the Ethics for an emotion, a state of being affected.

carryVoice: Your line: name it. One exact word can take a little heat out. Rest well.
